content: Patellar dislocation, which occurs when the kneecap (patella) completely disengages from the femoral groove (trochlear groove), affects up to 42 out of every 100,000 individuals. It is most commonly observed in people aged 20 to 30 years. There is ongoing uncertainty regarding whether surgical or non-surgical treatment is the optimal approach for managing this condition. This is a critical issue because up to 40% of individuals who experience a first-time (primary) patellar dislocation go on to have recurrent dislocations. Recurrent dislocations can significantly impair quality of life, often necessitating lifestyle modifications. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of surgical versus non-surgical interventions for treating individuals with either primary or recurrent patellar dislocation. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, AMED, CINAHL, and the Physiotherapy Evidence Database, as well as trial registries, in December 2021. Corresponding authors were also contacted to identify additional studies. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared surgical and non-surgical treatments for primary or recurrent lateral patellar dislocation in both adults and children. Standard Cochrane methods were employed for data collection and analysis. The primary outcomes assessed were recurrent patellar dislocation and patient-reported knee and physical function scores. Secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life, return to previous activities, knee pain (both during activity and at rest), adverse events, patient satisfaction, knee instability symptoms reported by patients, and the need for subsequent knee surgery. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 10 studies were included in the review, comprising eight randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and two quasi-RCTs, with a combined total of 519 participants. The mean ages of participants in the individual studies ranged from 13.0 to 27.2 years. Four studies included both children (primarily adolescents) and adults, while two studies exclusively recruited children. The follow-up periods for these studies ranged from one to 14 years. The certainty of the evidence for all outcomes was judged to be very low. This was due to several factors, including imprecision (fewer than 100 events reported or confidence intervals indicating both potential benefits and harms), risk of bias (high risk of performance, detection, and attrition bias in the studies), and inconsistency (high levels of statistical heterogeneity in pooled analyses). The evidence was inconclusive regarding whether surgery reduces the risk of recurrent dislocation following primary patellar dislocation compared to non-surgical management. For example, in the non-surgical group, the illustrative risk of recurrent dislocation was 348 per 1,000 individuals. Surgery was associated with 157 fewer cases of recurrent dislocation per 1,000 individuals (95% confidence interval: 209 fewer to 87 fewer) at two to nine years of follow-up. However, the certainty of this evidence was very low. Similarly, it is unclear whether surgery improves patient-reported knee and physical function scores. Various scales were used to measure this outcome, including the Tegner activity scale, the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, the Lysholm score, the Kujala Patellofemoral Disorders score, and the Hughston visual analogue scale. The Kujala score, the most frequently reported measure, suggested that individuals in the surgical group had a mean score 5.73 points higher at two to nine years of follow-up (95% confidence interval: 2.91 lower to 14.37 higher). On this 100-point scale, higher scores indicate better function, and a change of 10 points is considered clinically meaningful. However, the confidence interval includes the possibility of no meaningful improvement. The evidence was also uncertain regarding whether surgery increases the risk of adverse events. In the non-surgical group, the assumed risk of complications within the first two years was 277 per 1,000 individuals. In the surgical group, there were 335 more adverse events per 1,000 individuals (95% confidence interval: 75 fewer to 723 more). This finding was based on data from two studies involving 144 participants. Participant satisfaction was assessed in three studies (176 participants) at two to nine years of follow-up. There was little difference between the surgical and non-surgical groups. For example, in the non-surgical group, 763 per 1,000 participants reported excellent or good outcomes. In the surgical group, seven more participants per 1,000 (95% confidence interval: 199 fewer to 237 more) reported excellent or good satisfaction. Recurrent patellar subluxation was evaluated in four studies (256 participants) at two to nine years of follow-up. In the non-surgical group, the assumed risk of patellar subluxation was 292 per 1,000 individuals. Surgery was associated with 73 fewer cases of subluxation per 1,000 individuals (95% confidence interval: 146 fewer to 35 more). Slightly more individuals in the non-surgical group underwent subsequent surgery. Pooled data from three trials (195 participants) with two to nine years of follow-up indicated that, in the non-surgical group, the assumed risk of subsequent surgery was 215 per 1,000 individuals. Surgery was associated with 118 fewer cases of subsequent surgery per 1,000 individuals (95% confidence interval: 200 fewer to 372 more). In conclusion, the evidence is insufficient to determine whether surgery provides better outcomes than non-surgical management for patellar dislocation. The certainty of the evidence was very low across all outcomes. No adequately powered trials have specifically examined individuals with recurrent patellar dislocation. Future research should include well-designed, multicenter, randomized trials. To facilitate the design and implementation of such trials, expert consensus is needed to define the minimal descriptions of both surgical and non-surgical interventions, as well as the pathological variations that may influence the choice of treatment.
